lines.text: An illustration: on the first of every month, someone runs a revenue report on the production database.
Revenue per country, last quarter — it crawls through rows for many minutes.
Meanwhile, checkout slows down for every customer.
Same data, same SQL. So why is this query so painful?
lines.say: Same data, same S Q L. So why is this query so painful?

lines.text: By the end, you'll know where that report should run, why columns help, and how it can answer in seconds.
This video covers the second half of Chapter 3 of Martin Kleppmann's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
lines.say: This video covers the second half of Chapter three of Martin Klepman's book, Designing Data-Intensive Applications.

lines.text: Part 1 covered storage engines built to find a record by its key.
lines.say: Part one covered storage engines built to find a record by its key.

lines.text: This time, three questions. First: why do analytic queries need their own database?
Second: how should that database lay its data out on disk?
And third: can we avoid computing the same answer over and over again?
There are two broad kinds of database work: online transaction processing, OLTP, and online analytic processing, OLAP.
lines.say: There are two broad kinds of database work: online transaction processing, O L T P, and online analytic processing, O L A P.

lines.text: A transaction here just means a small group of reads and writes that must finish quickly.
Typically, OLTP reads a few rows by key; analytics aggregates over a huge number of rows.
lines.say: Typically, O L T P reads a few rows by key; analytics aggregates over a huge number of rows.

lines.text: OLTP writes are small and random, from user input; analytics gets bulk imports or event streams.
lines.say: O L T P writes are small and random, from user input; analytics gets bulk imports or event streams.

lines.text: Customers drive OLTP through the app; analysts use OLAP to make decisions.
lines.say: Customers drive O L T P through the app; analysts use O L A P to make decisions.

lines.text: OLTP holds the latest state; analytics holds the history of what happened.
lines.say: O L T P holds the latest state; analytics holds the history of what happened.

lines.text: OLTP data is typically gigabytes to terabytes; analytic data, terabytes to petabytes.
lines.say: O L T P data is typically gigabytes to terabytes; analytic data, terabytes to petabytes.

lines.text: Now run both on one database. The analyst's query scans a huge part of the table.
It competes for disk, memory, and CPU with the transactions customers are waiting on, so checkout slows down.
lines.say: It competes for disk, memory, and C P U with the transactions customers are waiting on, so checkout slows down.

lines.text: That's why people who operate OLTP databases are reluctant to let analysts run arbitrary queries on them.
lines.say: That's why people who operate O L T P databases are reluctant to let analysts run arbitrary queries on them.

lines.text: The fix is to give analytics its own database.
Part one, data warehousing. A data warehouse is a separate copy of your data, whose only job is answering analysts' questions about the business.
Picture a company with several OLTP systems: an orders database, a payments database, a support tool.
lines.say: Picture a company with several O L T P systems: an orders database, a payments database, a support tool.

lines.text: First, extract: pull data out of each one, either as a periodic dump or as a continuous stream of changes.
Then transform: clean it up and reshape it into a schema that's easy to analyze.
Finally, load it into the warehouse, which analysts can read but not write.
Extract, transform, load — together, that's called ETL.
lines.say: Extract, transform, load — together, that's called E T L.

lines.text: Now analysts can query as much as they like, and the systems serving customers don't feel a thing.
On the surface, a warehouse looks familiar: you talk to it with SQL, just like your OLTP database.
lines.say: On the surface, a warehouse looks familiar: you talk to it with S Q L, just like your O L T P database.

lines.text: Underneath, though, the internals are tuned for a completely different pattern: big scans instead of quick lookups by key.
As of the book in 2017, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, and ParAccel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted ParAccel.
lines.say: As of the book in twenty seventeen, commercial warehouses included Teradata, Vertica, S A P Hana, and Par Accel — Amazon Redshift is a hosted Par Accel.

lines.text: There were also open-source SQL-on-Hadoop engines, such as Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, and Presto.
lines.say: There were also open-source S Q L on Hadoop engines, such as Apache Hive, Spark S Q L, Cloudera Impala, and Presto.

lines.text: Same language on top, very different machinery below.
So what does the data look like inside a warehouse? Usually there's one big table in the middle, called the fact table.
Each row is one event — here, one payment — with values like the amount and the fee.
The other columns are keys pointing into smaller tables, called dimension tables.
Dimensions describe the who, what, where, when, and how of each event: the merchant, the payment method, the customer, the region.
Even the date is a dimension, so you can store facts like public holidays and filter on them.
Draw the dimensions around the fact table and you get a star, which is why it's called a star schema.
In real warehouses, fact tables are wide: often over 100 columns, sometimes several hundred.
lines.say: In real warehouses, fact tables are wide: often over one hundred columns, sometimes several hundred.

lines.text: And they get huge: the book describes big enterprises keeping tens of petabytes of transaction history, most of it in fact tables.
A variation, the snowflake schema, splits dimensions further into sub-dimensions — a merchant points to a category table and a country table.
That's more normalized, but stars are usually preferred because they're simpler for analysts to work with.
Part two, column storage. That wide fact table creates a problem, and the fix is to store data sideways, one column at a time.
Go back to our monthly report: total revenue per country, which needs only a handful of columns.
A typical warehouse query like this uses just 4 or 5 columns out of more than 100.
lines.say: A typical warehouse query like this uses just four or five columns out of more than one hundred.

lines.text: But most databases store data row by row: all the values of one row sit next to each other on disk.
So even with an index on the date, the database must load entire rows into memory and parse every column.
Then it throws away almost everything it just read.
A column store flips this: each column lives in its own file, and a query reads only the files it needs.
This only works if every file keeps the same order: the fourth entry in each file belongs to row four.
In this simplified illustration, we have 12 payments with 6 columns.
lines.say: In this simplified illustration, we have twelve payments with six columns.

lines.text: To add up the amounts for Germany, a row store reads all 72 cells, while a column store reads just two columns: 24 cells.
lines.say: To add up the amounts for Germany, a row store reads all seventy-two cells, while a column store reads just two columns: twenty-four cells.

lines.text: Now fetch one whole payment by its ID: both read 6 cells, but the column store has to visit 6 separate files.
lines.say: Now fetch one whole payment by its I D: both read six cells, but the column store has to visit six separate files.

lines.text: So columns win for scanning a few columns, and rows win for fetching whole records.
Careful with the name: column families in Cassandra and HBase still keep a row's values together, so they're mostly row-oriented.
lines.say: Careful with the name: column families in Cassandra and H Base still keep a row's values together, so they're mostly row-oriented.

lines.text: Storing columns separately has another bonus: they compress well, because a column's values tend to repeat.
Take the country column: DE, DE, DE, FR, FR, and so on.
lines.say: Take the country column: D E, D E, D E, F R, F R, and so on.

lines.text: It has only three distinct values across twelve rows.
The book gives a retailer with billions of sales but only 100,000 distinct products.
lines.say: The book gives a retailer with billions of sales but only one hundred thousand distinct products.

lines.text: So make one bitmap per value: a row of bits with a one wherever that row holds the value.
Each bitmap is mostly long runs, so we store only the run lengths, counting zeros first.
For DE, the list is 0, 3, 6, 2, 1.
lines.say: For D E, the list is zero, three, six, two, one.

lines.text: That's called run-length encoding.
With few distinct values and many rows, a whole column shrinks to a tiny list of numbers.
Bitmaps also make filters cheap. Say you want payments from Germany or the Netherlands.
Combine the DE and NL bitmaps with a bitwise OR: every row with a one in either bitmap matches.
lines.say: Combine the D E and N L bitmaps with a bitwise or: every row with a one in either bitmap matches.

lines.text: For a condition on two columns, like Germany and paid by card, you AND the country bitmap with the method bitmap — leaving exactly one row.
lines.say: For a condition on two columns, like Germany and paid by card, you and the country bitmap with the method bitmap — leaving exactly one row.

lines.text: That only works because every column stores its rows in the same order, so bit k always means row k.
lines.say: That only works because every column stores its rows in the same order, so bit kay always means row kay.

lines.text: When a query scans millions of rows, moving data becomes the bottleneck: first from disk into memory, then from memory into the CPU.
lines.say: When a query scans millions of rows, moving data becomes the bottleneck: first from disk into memory, then from memory into the C P U.

lines.text: Compressed columns help: one chunk of a column fits many rows' worth of values into the CPU's small, fast L1 cache.
lines.say: Compressed columns help: one chunk of a column fits many rows' worth of values into the C P U's small, fast L one cache.

lines.text: The CPU can then run a tight loop directly over that compressed chunk, like a bitwise AND, with no function call per row.
lines.say: The C P U can then run a tight loop directly over that compressed chunk, like a bitwise and, with no function call per row.

lines.text: This is called vectorized processing, and with SIMD instructions, one instruction can work on many values at once.
lines.say: This is called vectorized processing, and with sim dee instructions, one instruction can work on many values at once.

lines.text: Smaller data is faster to process, not just cheaper to store.
By default, rows are stored in the order they arrive, so the date column jumps around: 12 short runs.
lines.say: By default, rows are stored in the order they arrive, so the date column jumps around: twelve short runs.

lines.text: You can choose a sort order instead, but you can't sort each column on its own — you'd lose which amount belongs to which date.
So you sort whole rows, even though each column is stored separately.
Here, the sort key is date first, then merchant.
Now a query for June 2 reads only that block of rows and skips the rest.
lines.say: Now a query for June second reads only that block of rows and skips the rest.

lines.text: Sorting also helps compression: the date column collapses from 12 runs to 3, merchant has 8, and amount still has 12.
lines.say: Sorting also helps compression: the date column collapses from twelve runs to three, merchant has eight, and amount still has twelve.

lines.text: The first sort key compresses best; the further down the key, the more jumbled a column looks.
Warehouses keep several copies of the data anyway, so one machine failing doesn't lose anything.
So why not sort each copy differently: one by date, one by merchant, one by country?
Each query then uses the copy that fits it best — an idea from a research system called C-Store, adopted by Vertica.
lines.say: Each query then uses the copy that fits it best — an idea from a research system called C Store, adopted by Vertica.

lines.text: Unlike secondary indexes, which point to rows stored elsewhere, each sort order holds the actual column values.
There's a catch: all this sorting and compression makes writes hard.
You can't update in place like a B-tree, and inserting a row into the middle could mean rewriting every column file.
lines.say: You can't update in place like a B tree, and inserting a row into the middle could mean rewriting every column file.

lines.text: The fix comes from Part 1's LSM-trees: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.
lines.say: The fix comes from Part one's L S M trees: new writes go into a sorted buffer in memory first.

lines.text: When enough have piled up, they're merged with the column files and written out as new files, in bulk — Vertica does this.
Queries read both the files on disk and the buffer in memory and combine them, so a new write shows up right away.
Part three, precomputed aggregates — our last question: if the same totals get computed again and again, why not compute them once and keep them?
Warehouse queries keep asking for the same aggregates: counts, sums, averages, minimums, and maximums, often over the same grouping.
A normal, or virtual, view doesn't help here: it's just a saved query that runs again every time you read it.
A materialized view is different: it stores an actual copy of the query's result on disk, so reading it is cheap.
The cost is on writes: whenever the underlying data changes, the stored result has to be updated too.
That's why they're rare in OLTP databases, but in a warehouse, where reads dominate, they often make sense.
lines.say: That's why they're rare in O L T P databases, but in a warehouse, where reads dominate, they often make sense.

lines.text: A data cube is a special materialized view: a grid of totals grouped by dimensions — here, date by merchant.
In this simplified illustration, each cell sums one day's payments to one merchant, in thousands of dollars.
Summing a row gives that day's total, summing a column gives the merchant's total, and the grand total is 700 thousand.
lines.say: Summing a row gives that day's total, summing a column gives the merchant's total, and the grand total is seven hundred thousand.

lines.text: Add more dimensions and the grid becomes a cube; with five dimensions, it's a five-dimensional hypercube.
The upside: a question like Bolt's total across all days becomes a single lookup.
The downside: you can't ask about anything that isn't a dimension, like payments over $100, because amount isn't one.
lines.say: The downside: you can't ask about anything that isn't a dimension, like payments over one hundred dollars, because amount isn't one.

lines.text: So warehouses keep as much raw data as they can, and use cubes only to speed up common queries.
Back to the monthly report that slowed down checkout.
First, it shouldn't run on the production database at all: ETL copies the data into a warehouse, and checkout stays fast.
lines.say: First, it shouldn't run on the production database at all: E T L copies the data into a warehouse, and checkout stays fast.

lines.text: Second, it only needs a few columns, so a column store reads just those, compressed and sorted by date.
And third, totals that get asked for every month can be precomputed in a materialized view or a cube, so the report answers in seconds.
A few questions for your own system. Where do your heavy reports run: on the database serving your users, or on a copy built for analysis?
Which of your queries scan millions of rows but use only a few columns?
And which totals do you recompute on every dashboard load that could be computed once?
